etymologies.etymologyHTML: From roost +‎ -er. In the regions where it is used, displaced cock through taboo avoidance.

definitions.definition: (Canada, US, Kent, Australia, New Zealand) A male domestic chicken (Gallus gallus domesticus) or other gallinaceous bird.

quote.text: Their other dish  […]  contain'd a number of roast fowls—half a dozen, we suppose, & all roosters at this season no doubt.

quote.citation: 1836, Catharine Parr Traill, The Backwoods of Canada, page 308:
quote.text: The produce of two hens and a cock, or rooster, as the Yankees term that bird.

quote.citation: 1922 February, James Joyce, “[Episode 16]”, in Ulysses, Paris: Shakespeare and Company, […], →OCLC, part III [Nostos], page 616:
quote.text: Chalk a circle for a rooster.

definitions.definition: A bird or bat which roosts or is roosting.

quote.text: The more leisured flight of the roosters [sc. starlings] was in contrast to the steady procession of the migrants.

quote.citation: 1999, Milton W. Weller, Wetland Birds: Habitat Resources and Conservation Implications:
quote.text: Ground roosters like Northern Harriers may be subject to predation by Great-horned Owls  […]  but still larger perchers like herons and Ospreys use snags or posts in conspicuous places but are large enough to escape aerial predators.

definitions.definition: (figuratively, obsolete slang) A violent or disorderly person.
(figuratively) A powerful, prideful, or pompous person.
(figuratively, originally US slang, now chiefly New Zealand) A man.
(regional US, historical) A wild violet, when used in a children's game based on cockfighting.

quote.text: In April they played Hens and Roosters, yoking their wild white and blue violets to see which would get its head pulled off.

definitions.definition: (obsolete US slang) Legislation solely devised to benefit the legislators proposing it.

quote.text: American demoralisation... has carried rooster into the halls of republican legislation, where it indicates a bill or proposed law which will remunerate the legislators.
